enrichment.short_title: Bank claim for undervaluation of commercial property security
key_facts: Lloyds Bank instructed Edward Symmons to value the Sanderson Centre, Gosport, as security for a Salcrom Properties loan in September 1998.
Mr Skinner valued the property at £525,000; the bank sold its charge for that sum in December 1998 and later claimed true value was about £1.1m.
The bank's expert Mr Shores valued at £1,017,000 but the judge rejected his methodology as unreliable and doctrinaire.
Independent valuations by Mr Bannell (£540,000) and sensitivity analysis supported Skinner's figure as within a permissible non-negligent range.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of a bank's claim for breach of contract and negligence against surveyor valuers.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Skinner's valuation was held not to fall outside the permissible range of non-negligent valuations.
enrichment.ratio: A valuer is not negligent merely because another expert reaches a higher figure; where the defendant's valuation aligns with other competent valuations and the claimant's expert valuation is unreliable, the claim fails because negligence has not been established.
legal_issues: Whether Skinner negligently undervalued lettable space and income at the Sanderson Centre
Whether deductions for service costs and void accommodation were incompetent
Admissibility and weight of competing expert valuation evidence
Causation and loss where the bank sold security relying on the valuation

confidence.notes: Long TCC judgment with clear dismissal and detailed reasoning on expert valuation evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful licence recall after expired supervision period
key_facts: Rodgers was released on licence after serving half of a 13-year sentence but his licence wrongly stated supervision expired in February 2002 instead of 2005.
After common assault and affray offences in September 2002 the Secretary of State recalled him for breaching licence condition 5(vi) while under supervision.
Probation staff had told Rodgers supervision had ended and the recall letter relied solely on breach of supervision conditions, not unacceptable risk.
Hale LJ held recall for breach of expired supervision conditions was unlawful; ex post facto risk-based justifications were rejected.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Linked applications for habeas corpus and judicial review of a licence revocation and recall decision.
enrichment.outcome: Recall decision quashed; permission to appeal and stay refused; claimant entitled to release.
enrichment.ratio: The Secretary of State could not lawfully recall a long-term prisoner for breach of supervision conditions once the supervision period in the licence had expired; if recall for unacceptable risk was intended, that ground had to be stated at the time and properly explained, not rationalised afterwards.
legal_issues: Whether section 39 recall power applied after supervision had ended
Relationship between licence period and supervision period under section 37
Legitimate expectation and rationality of recall decision
Admissibility of later reasons explaining recall under ex parte Lillycrop principles

R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Lillycrop

enrichment.short_title: Unanimity required for hospital managers' discharge panel

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Tagoe-Thompson was detained under section 3 and requested review by three hospital managers under section 23(4).
The panel could not decide unanimously that he no longer met detention criteria and recorded that discharge was refused.
He argued section 23(4) allowed discharge by majority vote; the trust argued all three members had to agree to discharge.
The Court of Appeal held detention remained lawful because discharge required affirmative support from each of the three authorised members.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against refusal of habeas corpus and judicial review applications.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; subsequent detention following the panel decision was held lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 23(4) of the Mental Health Act 1983, where a panel of three members considers discharge, each member must support discharge before managers may override the responsible medical officer; the minimum of three is not merely a quorum for majority voting.
legal_issues: Construction of section 23(4) and whether managers act by majority or unanimity
Application of the Grindley v Barker presumption in mental health discharge decisions
Compatibility with Article 5 ECHR
Interaction with NHS trust committee quorum rules

enrichment.short_title: Date jobseeker's allowance ceases after failure to sign on
key_facts: Ferguson failed to attend and sign on at the Jobcentre on 1 June 1999 and next attended on 14 June 1999.
A Social Security Commissioner held JSA ceased on 1 June under regulation 26(c), not from 18/19 May under regulation 26(a).
The Secretary of State appealed, contending regulation 26(a) fixed cessation as the day after the last day for which entitlement was demonstrated.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding regulation 26(a) applied and entitlement ceased from 19 May 1999.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a Social Security Commissioner's decision on JSA cessation date.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declaration that Ferguson's JSA entitlement ceased from 19 May 1999 and was not payable to 13 June 1999.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 26(a) of the Jobseeker's Allowance Regulations 1996 operates where a claimant fails to attend or sign on, fixing cessation at the day after the last day in respect of which he provided information or evidence showing continuing entitlement; it does not render regulations 26(b) and (c) devoid of meaning.
legal_issues: Construction of regulation 26(a) versus 26(b) and 26(c)
Distinction between cessation events under regulation 25 and cessation dates under regulation 26
Whether failure to provide a declaration falls within regulation 26(a) or only 26(c)
Effect of JSA being paid fortnightly in arrears

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory construction judgment with clear declaration on the correct cessation date.

enrichment.short_title: Limitation for negligence in delayed accountant litigation
key_facts: Hatton instructed Chafes in 1984 to pursue accountants for losses from 1983; the underlying claim was struck out for want of prosecution in June 1999.
He issued a professional negligence claim against the solicitors in October 2000, alleging failure to progress the accountants action.
The judge had left limitation unclear; the Court of Appeal held the underlying claim was worthless by October 1994 with no arguable defence to strike-out.
Section 14A knowledge was found by October/November 1995 when solicitor Mr Roberts conceded he could not defend another strike-out application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against refusal to strike out a solicitor negligence claim on limitation grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; action declared time barred and dismissed; proposed amendment refused.
enrichment.ratio: In solicitor negligence claims arising from delay, damage accrues when the underlying claim becomes doomed to failure, not only when it is actually struck out; following Khan v Falvey, where there was no arguable defence to strike-out by October 1994 the six-year period had expired and section 14A knowledge existed by late 1995.
legal_issues: When a cause of action accrues for negligent litigation delay
Application of Hopkins v McKenzie after Khan v Falvey and Nykredit
Whether the claim was worthless before actual strike-out in 1999
Section 14A starting date for knowledge of solicitors' negligence

linked_authorities.name: Nykredit Mortgage Bank Plc v Edward Erdman Group Ltd (No 2)

enrichment.short_title: Workplace stroke after load bar struck driver's head
key_facts: Russell, a Wincanton lorry driver, alleged unsecured load bars slid out when he opened trailer doors on 17/18 June 1998, glancing his left temple.
He suffered dysphasia and a stroke linked to a pre-existing diseased carotid artery; a further major stroke followed on 1 July 1998.
Contemporaneous accident records were inconsistent, but the judge accepted evidence from his wife, colleague McKenna and Mr Marsden.
The Court of Appeal upheld liability findings, including that head flexion to the right was highly likely despite inconsistent witness demonstrations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal against High Court entry of judgment on liability with damages to be assessed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; liability judgment upheld with costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge makes clear credibility findings in a fact-sensitive workplace injury case and medical evidence supports causation, an appellate court will not interfere merely because contemporaneous records were inconsistent or the claimant's recollection of head movement was unreliable.
legal_issues: Whether the head injury was caused by a load bar emerging from the trailer
Causation between glancing blow and carotid artery damage triggering stroke
Effect of dysphasia on reliability of contemporaneous accident accounts
Whether the judge impermissibly speculated on direction of head movement

confidence.notes: Full liability appeal judgment with detailed fact findings and medical evidence analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Wasted costs application against claimant solicitors rejected
key_facts: Afzal brought a legally aided personal injury claim against Chubb after an alleged workplace attack; preliminary issues on psychiatric injury and disability were tried in March 2002.
The judge revoked the litigation friend, dismissed the action, and the defendants applied for wasted costs against former solicitors Iliffe Booth Bennett.
Defendants alleged negligent handling of medical evidence meant the preliminary issue trial should never have proceeded.
The judge rejected the application, finding IBB were not negligent and counsel's assessment that Dr Bhatti-Ali's evidence remained arguable was reasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second-stage wasted costs application under section 51 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 and CPR Part 48.
enrichment.outcome: Wasted costs application rejected; solicitors held not negligent and any failings did not cause loss.
enrichment.ratio: A wasted costs order requires clear proof of improper, unreasonable or negligent conduct causing unnecessary costs; solicitors acting for legally aided claimants in a difficult medical case may rely on counsel's advice and are not negligent simply because expert evidence later fails at trial.
legal_issues: Jurisdiction and procedure for wasted costs orders under CPR 48 PD53
Whether solicitors negligently failed to disclose or share medical reports with experts
Causation if better case management might have led to withdrawal of legal aid
Standard of negligence for legally aided personal injury solicitors

confidence.notes: Detailed wasted costs judgment applying Ridehalgh principles with clear rejection of negligence allegations.

enrichment.short_title: Council tax liability for investment property owner

statutes_considered.title: Valuation and Community Charge Tribunals Regulations 1989

key_facts: Bennett owned Woodville Cottage in Cumbria as an investment property rented to tenants while living mainly in Bedford and elsewhere for work.
Copeland Borough Council determined he was council tax liable as resident freehold owner under section 6(2)(a).
The valuation tribunal found the cottage was his sole or main residence because he had no other property interest and intended to retire there.
The High Court dismissed his appeal on a point of law, rejecting late tenancy agreements and upholding discount findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a point of law from a Valuation Tribunal council tax liability decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal decision confirmed; claimant ordered to pay respondent's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Residence for council tax depends on all circumstances, not time spent at the dwelling alone; an owner with freehold interest, right to return, occasional visits and retirement intention may be 'resident' even if living nomadically elsewhere and never having lived at the property.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'sole or main residence' under section 6(5) of the 1992 Act
Whether tenants with exclusive possession displaced owner liability
Admissibility of late tenancy agreements on appeal under Ladd v Marshall
Challenge to tribunal discount findings

enrichment.short_title: Representative BPI claim against parallel CD imports
key_facts: Record companies sued operators of the CD-WOW website for importing genuine non-EEA CDs into the UK, infringing UK sound recording copyright.
Claimants sought to sue on behalf of all relevant BPI and PPL members owning or exclusively licensing UK copyrights.
Defendants applied under CPR 19.6(2) to prevent representative proceedings for lack of same interest and authority.
The Vice-Chancellor held members shared a common interest and grievance and refused to direct that claimants could not act as representatives.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications on representative capacity under CPR Rule 19.6 and permission to amend/add claimants.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants' application under CPR 19.6(2) dismissed; representative claim permitted subject to amendment directions.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 19.6 does not require prior authority from represented persons; where record company members share the same interest in restraining identical parallel-import infringements and the same legal issues arise, a representative claim is a flexible and convenient tool that may proceed.
legal_issues: Whether claimants and BPI/PPL members had the same interest under CPR 19.6(1)
Whether representative claimants required members' authority to sue
Scope of injunctive and pecuniary relief in a representative copyright action
Whether defendants should be protected from uncertain representative proceedings

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural judgment on representative actions with clear application of CPR 19.6 principles.

enrichment.short_title: Whole quashing of mink fur farming compensation order
key_facts: Mink fur farmers challenged the 2002 compensation scheme made under the Fur Farming (Prohibition) Act 2000.
Stanley Burnton J had held provisions for compensation for residual breeding stock unlawful in his principal judgment.
The Secretary of State argued for partial severance so other payments could continue; claimants sought quashing of the whole order.
The judge quashed the entire order, finding income and breeding-stock compensation interdependent and the statutory duty to make a fair scheme unfulfilled.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Post-judgment hearing on form of quashing order, costs and permission to appeal after successful judicial review of a statutory compensation scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Whole compensation order quashed; claimants awarded 85% of legal costs capped at £40,000 plus surveyors' costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where compensation for loss of income and for breeding stock are interdependent parts of a single statutory scheme, partial severance is inappropriate; quashing the whole order preserves the Secretary of State's duty to make a fresh rational and fair compensation scheme.
legal_issues: Whether unlawful breeding-stock provisions could be severed from the remainder of the compensation order
Interdependence of income-based and stock-based compensation heads
Whether remaining provisions could satisfy section 5 without fresh consultation
Costs apportionment where some judicial review grounds failed or were abandoned
